title: Soil Resource Heterogeneity Shapes the Scale-Dependence of Functional Diversity and Species-Functional Diversity Relationships During Karst Abandoned Farmland Restoration
content: Karst ecosystems are characterized by thin, discontinuous soils and high resource het-erogeneity. With widespread farmland abandonment, understanding biodiversity and functional recover during early succession is critical for evaluating restoration in these fragile landscapes. Functional diversity (FD) complements species diversity (SD) in re-flecting ecosystem processes, yet how soil resource heterogeneity shapes FD across spa-tial scales, and whether the SD-FD relationship shifts with scale, remains unclear in karst abandoned farmland. Here, we used a four-year fenced permanent plot to examine scale-dependent relationships among soil resource heterogeneity, herbaceous FD, the SD-FD relationship, and the potential pathways linking resource heterogeneity to FD. Results showed that: (1) a significant positive relationship between soil resource heter-ogeneity and FD emerged only at the largest spatial scale examined (15 m × 15 m); (2) the SD-FD relationship shifted from positive at small scales to negative at larger scales, with functional redundancy potentially contributing to the negative relationship; (3) Soil resource heterogeneity was linked to FD through both interspecific trait differences and species diversity, with the relative importance of these pathways varying across scales. Our findings demonstrate strong scale dependence in relationships between soil re-source heterogeneity and FD, and show that the SD-FD relationship can shift direction during early succession. By highlighting the scale-dependent roles of resource hetero-geneity, trait differentiation, and functional redundancy, this study provides new evi-dence that soil resource heterogeneity is associated with community functional structure through changes in trait and species components. These findings emphasize the need to incorporate multiscale diversity metrics into restoration assessments.
